findings.title: Shortcut hotstring auto-close is admitted but never closes its Linux page
findings.reproduction: Open the hotstring editor through its shortcut, enable auto_close, add one entry and save without the Add another option. Shared script.js:1290-1293 posts close after persist. Alternatively route that exact {action:'close',data:{}} from a current hsEditor page. Replay probes/editor.lua SOURCE_ROOT: CLOSE_RECEIPT close_calls=0 reply=nil despite an accepting exact close_owned_window capability. This is a bridge/native-port model, not live GTK measurement.
findings.root_cause: linux/ui/hotstring_editor/bridge.lua:694-697 recognizes close but only logs 'closed' and returns nil; it never calls the manager-supplied epoch-owned context.close_owned_window. Therefore the registered route cannot reach native hide/destroy or input ownership release for this admitted command.
findings.silent_failure: The handler logs that the editor closed even though no close was requested. Existing opening-source tests verify saves, while native lifecycle tests verify hide once invoked; neither joins the shared auto-close command to this handler.
findings.regression_test: Use the actual manager and bridge with faithful GTK ports. Open shortcut mode with auto_close, deliver the shared page's close command, require exactly one close of the current page, physical retirement acknowledgements and input release. Refused native retirement must retain debt and report refusal; stale close must not retire a successor. Healthy manual window close is the control.
findings.other_os: macOS ui/hotstring_editor/init.lua handle_message close calls M.close. Windows has a distinct personal-TOML editor, so the same API is not owed; its exact corresponding shortcut close join is outside this Linux proof. The separate shared page's premature close before save acknowledgement is coordinated with the macOS reviewer.

findings.title: Hotstring save reports success after the real catalogue reload refuses
findings.reproduction: Initialize the actual Config and hotstring_engine on private personal.toml; display the actual editor model; create a new malformed second TOML with no healthy cached snapshot; save an edit to personal.toml. The canonical writer commits the edit, actual Config.reload returns count,false and the engine generation remains unchanged, but the bridge returns saved=true with zero UI alerts. probes/editor.lua proves this plus healthy, refused-receipt and throwing reload controls. No business reload/engine/writer is mocked in the actual refusal case; the host is a recording native port.
findings.root_cause: linux/ui/hotstring_editor/bridge.lua:469-475 records only pcall(config.reload)'s first boolean and ignores the actual committed receipt. save_all then returns true at494 even when reload refuses or raises. Config.reload at1655-1661 faithfully returns load_all's count,committed,cause; the bridge discards that existing contract.
findings.silent_failure: For a nonthrowing refusal only central catalogue logs describe the failure. The editor takes the successful save branch and sends no save_error alert; its shared page independently flashes saved immediately. On a throw, only a warning is emitted and saved=true still returns. Personal-info bridge already checks reload's committed receipt correctly.
findings.regression_test: Drive a real private catalogue and editor: introduce a new malformed source after display, save the editable source, assert its bytes committed but the engine's old generation remains and the user receives explicit saved-but-not-reloaded failure. Require healthy reload to publish the new generation, and cover false/nil/throw receipts. Keep persistence truth separate from live publication and coordinate the shared page acknowledgement fix.
findings.other_os: macOS ui/hotstring_editor/init.lua validates reload_toml's returned committed boolean and notifies on refusal. Windows has its own personal-TOML save path; exact native parity remains with its reviewer. The common immediate saved toast is a shared page root, not counted a second time here.
